earthquakeFunFacts.fact: Every day, Earth experiences around 55 earthquakes every hour. Most are too small for humans to notice.
The largest earthquake ever recorded was the 1960 Valdivia Earthquake in Chile at magnitude 9.5.
Earthquakes can make the ground move faster than a Formula 1 race car.
Some earthquakes last only a few seconds, while others can continue for several minutes.
Japan records thousands of earthquakes every year due to its location on multiple tectonic plate boundaries.
Animals have been reported behaving strangely before some earthquakes, though scientists still debate why.
The deepest recorded earthquake occurred about 700 kilometers beneath Earth's surface.
Earthquakes can temporarily change the length of a day by altering Earth's rotation.
A magnitude 8 earthquake releases about 32 times more energy than a magnitude 7.
The ground can crack open during powerful earthquakes, but movie-style giant chasms are rare.
Underwater earthquakes can generate tsunamis that travel across entire oceans.
The Pacific Ring of Fire is responsible for about 90% of the world's earthquakes.
Earthquakes can trigger landslides, avalanches, and even volcanic activity.
Scientists use seismic waves to study Earth's hidden interior.
A foreshock is a smaller earthquake that happens before a larger one.
Aftershocks can continue for days, months, or even years after a major quake.
The strongest shaking is not always directly above the epicenter.
Earthquakes have been detected on the Moon.
Mars experiences marsquakes, proving earthquakes aren't unique to Earth.
Some earthquakes are caused by human activities such as mining and reservoir filling.
The first seismometer was invented in China nearly 2,000 years ago.
Earthquakes can create new lakes by altering river paths.
The sound some people hear during earthquakes often comes from vibrating structures and ground movement.
Large earthquakes can permanently shift coastlines.
The 2004 Indian Ocean earthquake shortened Earth's day by a tiny fraction of a second.
Some faults stay quiet for centuries before producing a major earthquake.
Earthquakes can occur in every season and every type of weather.
Weather does not cause tectonic earthquakes.
The term 'Ring of Fire' refers to a horseshoe-shaped zone around the Pacific Ocean.
The Philippines sits within the Pacific Ring of Fire, making earthquakes common.
Earthquakes can make buildings sway even when people don't feel the shaking.
A seismic gap is an area that hasn't experienced a major earthquake for an unusually long time.
Liquefaction can make solid ground behave like a liquid during strong shaking.
Earthquakes have caused entire neighborhoods to sink several feet.
The Richter Scale is famous, but scientists now mostly use Moment Magnitude.
Seismic waves can travel through the entire planet.
P-waves are the fastest earthquake waves and arrive first.
S-waves cannot travel through liquid, helping scientists identify Earth's liquid outer core.
Some skyscrapers are designed to sway safely during earthquakes.
Earthquake-resistant buildings don't stop shaking; they survive it.
Certain bridges can move several feet during major earthquakes without collapsing.
The San Andreas Fault is over 1,200 kilometers long.
Most earthquakes occur less than 70 kilometers below the surface.
Deep earthquakes are often felt over wider areas than shallow ones.
Earthquakes can trigger fires by damaging gas lines and electrical systems.
The deadliest earthquake in history may have killed more than 800,000 people in China in 1556.
Modern earthquake early warning systems can provide a few seconds of notice before strong shaking arrives.
A few seconds of warning can stop trains and open fire station doors automatically.
Earthquakes cannot currently be predicted with exact dates and times.
Scientists can identify regions at risk, but not the precise moment a quake will occur.
The ocean floor is constantly moving due to plate tectonics.
Subduction zones produce many of the world's strongest earthquakes.
Megathrust earthquakes occur where one tectonic plate dives beneath another.
Some underwater earthquakes are so powerful they move entire sections of the seafloor.
A major earthquake can raise coastal land several meters almost instantly.
Tectonic uplift from earthquakes can expose coral reefs above sea level.
Earthquakes can alter groundwater levels in wells.
Some lakes have sloshed like giant bathtubs during earthquakes.
Earthquakes release energy accumulated over decades, centuries, or even millennia.
A magnitude 9 earthquake releases roughly 1,000 times more energy than a magnitude 7.
The strongest shaking is usually near the fault rupture, not necessarily the epicenter.
The epicenter is just the surface point above where the rupture starts underground.
Scientists locate earthquakes using arrival times from multiple seismic stations.
Three seismic stations are the minimum needed to pinpoint an epicenter accurately.
Some faults creep slowly without producing large earthquakes.
Earthquakes can occasionally trigger other earthquakes hundreds of kilometers away.
Large earthquakes have been known to shake the entire planet.
Sensitive instruments can detect earthquakes from the opposite side of Earth.
The ground can move vertically, horizontally, or both during a quake.
Not all faults produce visible cracks at the surface.
Earthquake lights have occasionally been reported before or during major earthquakes.
Scientists are still studying the cause of earthquake lights.
The 2011 Japan earthquake shifted the main island several meters eastward.
That same earthquake generated a devastating Pacific-wide tsunami.
Earthquakes can permanently alter maps.
The largest fault ruptures can extend for over 1,000 kilometers.
Seismologists sometimes call Earth a giant bell because large earthquakes make it vibrate globally.
Earth's crust is broken into giant moving tectonic plates.
Those plates move about as fast as human fingernails grow.
Every earthquake tells a story about how our planet is constantly changing beneath our feet.
